items.title: Yum China CEO Joey Wat: What China’s consumer market can teach global business
items.summary:
In 1987, KFC opened its first restaurant in Beijing, marking the debut of China’s first Western quick-service restaurant brand. Nearly four decades later, KFC China has expanded to more than 14,000 stores in a market that has transformed around it.

KFC has changed alongside it. In addition to the Original Recipe Chicken and Zinger, our menu offers energy bowls and sparkling coffee – many of which cannot be found in KFC menus outside China. More broadly, we have adapted everything from marketing to store formats as consumer preferences, technology and competition have evolved.

For any global brand, keeping pace with such change requires tremendous effort. I believe one reason KFC has been able to keep adapting is the strength of our local teams. They have the know-how and autonomy to respond to the market with agility. The brand may be global, but decisions are made close to the consumer.

KFC is one of the six restaurant brands operated by Yum China , which together span 20,000 stores across the country. Our experience, including 10 years as a company listed on the New York Stock Exchange, has reinforced three lessons for global brands seeking to win in this market. While shaped in China, I believe they extend far beyond it.

First, a dual focus on innovation and efficiency is essential to survival and prosperity. 

One fundamental reality about China is that it is not a single market, but many. Consumer preferences, consumption occasions and competitive landscapes vary across regions and city tiers. A single playbook is not enough to win, which is why we tailor store…
items.t: Yum China CEO Joey Wat: What China’s consumer market can teach global business

items.title: ‘Wolf of Wall Street’ Jordan Belfort on his AI salespeople who are better than humans: ‘What if you have a bad apple that says stuff?’
items.summary:
Just months after Jordan Belfort’s court-ordered restitution obligation ended, leaving his victims far short of the $110 million he was ordered to pay them, “The Wolf of Wall Street” is selling over the phone again, this time with AI bots trained on his sales techniques.

Belfort’s new AI sales-voice startup, Tone, has brought in about $1 million in revenue so far, and he’s aiming for between $20 million and $30 million in recurring revenue within the next year.

Belfort said Tone’s technology is more reliable than humans because companies can keep a firm grip on what it says. This contrasts with salespeople who can stray from approved scripts and could potentially cross a line with customers.

“What if you have a bad apple that says stuff—maybe inadvertently even, right?” he said.

Tone launched publicly on Nov. 16 with about $10 million raised, and Belfort said its API and a content creation platform goes live in about a week. It arrives as big companies move to automate customer calls— Verizon CEO Dan Schulman told Fortune this month the telecom giant is preparing to automate much of its routine customer service work—and two years after the FCC put AI-generated voices under federal robocall rules. A study by international cloud voice software company AVOXI found in September that just over half of organizations are already using AI voice agents, and a majority are planning to adopt them over the next two years.

Tone’s offerings include 16 different male and female artificial voices ranging from higher to lower-pitched that are trained on Belfort’s tonal sales…
items.t: ‘Wolf of Wall Street’ Jordan Belfort on his AI salespeople who are better than humans: ‘What if you have a bad apple that says stuff?’

items.title: Nvidia raised next year’s sales target by tens of billions of dollars, signaling confidence in its future without Jensen Huang
items.summary:
Nvidia raised its sales forecast for fiscal 2028, and reported stronger-than-expected results in its most recent quarter, in a striking signal of business confidence by the AI chipmaker following the resignation of longtime CEO and cofounder Jensen Huang .

“Our momentum is real,” interim CEO Colette Kress said on conference call with analysts on Tuesday, citing strong demand for the company’s products, Nvidia’s ongoing technological advances, and the commitment of its employees. Kress, Nvidia’s longtime finance chief, made her debut as interim CEO on Tuesday’s earnings call, flanked by newly appointed Chair of the board Harvey Jones. 

The pair took pains to project a business-as-usual attitude—even using the phrase—while seeking to put Huang in the rear-view mirror. The board of directors “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Jones said at the start of the call, noting that the company has retained executive recruiting firm Hedrick & Struggles to search for a permanent CEO. 

The comments were a direct rebuttal to Huang, who is seeking to reclaim the CEO throne days after resigning amid revelations of multiple affairs, one reportedly with a Nvidia employee and another with a woman some believe may be a Chinese spy.

Shares of Nvidia were up more than 4% in after hours trading on Tuesday. The company’s stock has plummeted more than 36% in the past month, shedding more than a trillion dollars in market value.

Nvidia said Tuesday that revenue in three months ended October 25 totaled $115.8 billion, roughly twice the amount it generated in the year ago period, and…
items.t: Nvidia raised next year’s sales target by tens of billions of dollars, signaling confidence in its future without Jensen Huang

items.title: Optum’s CEO still works weekends as a pediatrician. What he sees ‘should not happen in America, but it does every single day’
items.summary:
On his last couple of weekends working as a hospital pediatrician in Boston, Dr. Patrick Conway saw three patients he can’t stop talking about.

One was a 14-year-old girl who had called more than 100 people trying to get mental health care before she ended up in his hospital with broken legs. Another was a 21-year-old with meningitis. “She wakes up. What’s the first thing she says? I’m a single mother. I can’t afford this. I got to get out of here,” Conway said. The third was a 15-year-old on Medicaid who needed complex rehab for a neurologic disorder, and the hospital was struggling to find anywhere to send her.

“That should not happen in America, but it does every single day,” he said.

During the week, Conway runs Optum, the health services arm of UnitedHealth Group, which he said employs about 300,000 of the conglomerate’s roughly 400,000 people. That makes him one of the more unusual witnesses to American health care’s failures, because his company sits on the other side of many of them. Speaking at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Monday, he told Fortune’s Diane Brady that the weekend shifts are the point. “Those stories could be anywhere in America,” he said, and Optum’s job is “to prevent those stories from occurring in the future.”

Brady put the tension more bluntly. Optum, she said, is a bit like the cable guy: people need it, and they don’t always love it. Conway didn’t argue with that. He said Optum’s business customers (health systems, payers, employers) are “generally quite positive.” On the insurance side, “people have concerns,” he said,…
items.t: Optum’s CEO still works weekends as a pediatrician. What he sees ‘should not happen in America, but it does every single day’

items.title: If it looks like a DDoS attack
items.summary:
In five days, three pillars of American life stopped working. On Thursday, Nov. 12, Microsoft Outlook went down worldwide, drawing more than 43,000 problem reports from 72 countries by the next morning in an outage that ran past 12 hours. On Friday, the FAA halted every departure in the country for more than four hours after its communications network failed; nearly 12,000 flights were canceled and the backlog was still felt days later. On Monday, customers of Chase, Bank of America , Wells Fargo , U.S. Bank and Truist found themselves locked out of online banking, with Chase alone drawing more than 5,000 outage reports by early afternoon.

Each organization was quick to say what it was not: an attack.

Microsoft: “ There is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity .” Chase: “ This is a technical issue, not cyber related .” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a “ nefarious attack ” on the FAA.

But look at what each one describes. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said, “ Our switches, our routers, actually got overloaded with data ,” after a newly installed router fired roughly 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. A flood of requests overwhelming network equipment until legitimate traffic cannot get through is not merely similar to a denial-of-service attack. It is the textbook definition of one. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford has said that explanation does not fully account for the root cause. Microsoft has blamed a network upgrade but has not published a full post-incident report. Chase…
items.t: If it looks like a DDoS attack

items.title: Microsoft’s Satya Nadella praises Jensen Huang, says return as CEO is ‘up to the Nvidia board’
items.summary:
Microsoft Chief Executive Satya Nadella praised ousted Nvidia founder Jensen Huang as “a singular person” who has contributed immensely to the tech industry, but he stopped short of calling for Huang’s reinstatement to the chipmaker’s top job.

“I just want to give him space for what he needs to do there, and it’s not up to me. It’s up to the Nvidia board to decide what happens next,” Nadella said Tuesday at a media roundtable in San Francisco during Microsoft’s Ignite conference. He added that he had “all the admiration, respect for what Jensen has done for this industry, and what he’s done for Nvidia,” noting that he has known and worked with Huang for a long time.

Huang, who turned Nvidia into the dominant maker of AI chips and owns about a 3.56% stake, on Thursday stepped down as CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago, amid revelations of multiple affairs, including one with an executive whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of being a Chinese spy. On Tuesday morning, Huang broke his silence and said he would be open to returning as CEO . Later in the day, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones said the company did not intend to bring Huang back.

Nadella, who said he texted Huang over the weekend to say he was thinking of him, said that Nvidia has a deep bench of talent.

“I think Nvidia does have a lot of human capital and very capable leadership,” Nadella said, noting that interim CEO and Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress once worked at Microsoft. “I’m making sure that we have the same type of partnership, and we’re scaling Rubins as we speak,” Nadella said,…
items.t: Microsoft’s Satya Nadella: Jensen Huang ‘a singular person,’ but it’s up to Nvidia to decide whether to bring him back as CEO

items.title: Altria CEO says ‘responsibility needs to be at the heart’ of its FDA-regulated nicotine business. It’s part of why it sued the regulator

As Big Tobacco companies pivot away from combustible products to less harmful nicotine alternatives, they’re finding new challenges in their relationships with regulators.

Sal Mancuso, the CEO of Altria Group, which owns cigarette and cigar brands like Marlboro and Black & Mild, explained at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Monday that competing in a Food and Drug Administration-regulated industry brings with it both an added sense of responsibility to consumers, and hurdles in competing with other businesses in the space. Mancuso said that Altria’s On! nicotine pouch brand is a key innovation for the company, but regulations have slowed growth.

The Marlboro-maker announced its Moving Beyond Smoking initiative in 2023 as more consumers move away from cigarettes, putting a renewed focus on smoke-free alternatives to cigarettes such as NJOY vapes and On! nicotine pouches, which are competing with Philip Morris’s Zyn. 

“You can call us the underdog in the pouch category today, but our intention is to lead the pouch category over the long term,” Mancuso told Fortune Executive Editorial Director Diane Brady. “When you think about what’s maybe getting in the way, there’s a couple of factors: One is just the misperception that nicotine is what causes harm from tobacco use. Most of the harm is from combustion, so clarifying that misperception is important. And then we are regulated by the FDA. When you’re in the nicotine business, responsibility needs to be at the heart of everything you do.” 

Altria, through its subsidiaries Helix Innovations and NJOY, sued the…
items.t: Altria CEO says ‘responsibility needs to be at the heart’ of its FDA-regulated nicotine business. It’s part of why it sued the regulator

items.title: The Guardian view on the Milburn report: a manifesto for youth participation | Editorial
items.summary:
This is not a rerun of failed welfare cuts, but young people who rely on benefits cannot be expected to take promised opportunities on trust

The gap between the state’s investment in young people compared with older generations has more than doubled in two decades. At the same time, the number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are neither in education, employment or training (Neet) has climbed to 1 million. In Europe, only Romania has a higher Neet rate.

Alan Milburn’s message is that this amounts to a “moral crisis” which the British state must urgently address. Asked to write a review about young people and work, he has produced a “manifesto” for placing the broken social contract between generations at the heart of government. On Tuesday, his proposals for far-reaching changes to welfare, health, education and employment were on their way to becoming government policy as he was chosen to lead a new Youth Opportunities Unit.

items.title: The Guardian view on climate debt: a vicious cycle the world must break at Cop31 | Editorial
items.summary:
Poor countries are paying creditors instead of preparing for climate disasters. The international financial system must stop deepening their vulnerability

The catastrophe that struck Nepal’s Himalayas in August began with a collapsing glacier. An avalanche of ice and rock unleashed deadly floods, sweeping away villages, bridges and roads, and leaving thousands dead or missing. It illustrated the dangers posed by global heating to the Himalayas’ increasingly unstable glaciers. Nepal lost a tenth of its electricity generation. Reconstruction will cost about $5bn. Yet the Loss and Damage Fund, hailed as a historic breakthrough at the 2022 UN climate summit, has earmarked just $20m for Nepal – less than 5% of the $482m that Kathmandu must pay its external public creditors this year.

items.title: Will the Milburn review come good or go south? Either way, we’ll always have Eurovision

The announcement of state plans to engage with young people told us nothing we hadn’t already heard, but it still felt momentous

It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over.

Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans.

But Kalshi is turning that workplace distraction into a high-paying new job. The $40 billion prediction market giant is hiring a “GTA VI Researcher” to play through the entirety of the highly anticipated game .

“We’re looking for someone whose parents said video games would never pay the bills. They were wrong, and you can tell them we said so,” the job listing stated .

The gig comes with a hefty paycheck: a $100,00 to $120,000 fixed project fee, plus an additional $15,000 completion bonus. The successful applicant will begin playing at midnight on November 19—livestreaming with camera via YouTube or Twitch—and continue until beating the game’s story mode. 

Exactly how long that will take will vary by player. Rob Nelson, who oversaw the game’s development at Rockstar Games , told The New York Times that his own playthrough in Leonida—the game’s fictional U.S. state name—took about 80 hours, including the main story and some optional side quests.

“I hope that there will be people that want to get up, have a cup of coffee, shower, get dressed, go out for a little exercise,” Nelson said.

Kalshi has explicitly noted that “sleep and touching grass are both allowed,” meaning the researcher won’t have to power through the game in one sitting. But playing through the story is only part of the assignment.

Kalshi’s $135,000 “GTA VI” job has attracted more than 25,000 applicants

items.title: The corporate boom in vegan food is dead. Long live real plant-based cooking | Isobel Lewis
items.summary:
The fad for plant-based junk food has run its course, but restaurants reflecting the centuries-long history of this cuisine still thrive

Have you ever gone to make a restaurant reservation and been met with a Google Maps listing bearing that harbinger of doom: “Permanently closed”? It’s a pretty deflating feeling – and one the UK’s vegan population knows well. Over the past few years, many once-beloved, plant-based establishments have shut up shop or moved away from brick-and-mortar businesses, from The Allotment in Manchester to The Vurger Co, which had restaurants in London and Brighton. Each shuttering galvanises the vegan community into supporting their local spots. But they’re gutting too, and deeply felt by a group who see themselves more as an ethically motivated community than simply clientele.

The so-called sorry state of the vegan restaurant scene has been widely reported on (not least by me). items.title: Can this experimental orchard save the UK’s cider industry?
items.summary:
Farmers are utilising science and nature to help orchards adapt and thrive in the face of shifting temperatures, rainfall and pests

On Myrtle Farm in Somerset, there are thousands of apple trees laid out in rows of 100. Over the past year, each has endured the same wet winter and long summer drought. Now, the different ways each tree responded to these challenges are being analysed in trials that could shape the future of apple growing – and the taste of cider – for decades to come.

Myrtle Farm is the home of Thatchers Cider, which this year had its earliest ever harvest in the company’s 122-year history. Yet the farm’s experimental orchard of 3,800 trees, where each 100-tree row produces a different apple variety, offers hope that – even as the climate emergency deepens – future harvests will become more consistent and predictable.

Two apples ripe for harvest, which this year ran from the middle of August to November at Myrtle Farm

items.t: Drought, early harvests and wet winters: can an experimental orchard save the UK’s cider industry?

items.title: Millionaire factory: Anthropic IPO set to fuel AI gold rush in London’s high-end property market
items.summary:
New tech wealth, amassed with remarkable speed, is now washing up on British shores

Sporting hoodies and white trainers rather than the gilets of London’s banker and lawyer class, tech bros can struggle to be taken seriously by the capital’s luxury property agents. “We worked with a young tech entrepreneur with a substantial budget, who agents assumed was looking to rent a one-bedroom flat,” says Jo Eccles, a buying agent who sources off-market properties for ultra-wealthy clients.

But this week’s float by Anthropic, the AI developer behind the chatbot Claude, promises to bring even more credibility for the growing cohort of tech millionaires, which could breathe life into London’s ailing high-end property market. Its IPO on Thursday, expected to value the company at $1.4tn (£1.1tn), is likely to turn more than 4,000 of its staff into millionaires as their stock options vest. SaaStr, a California research firm, has estimated that the minimum value generated for staff at the AI lab will be $20m each.

items.title: Sam Bankman-Fried’s former employer Jane Street poised for $35 billion windfall from purchase of Anthropic shares in FTX bankruptcy
items.summary:
When Anthropic goes public this week, several big players will enjoy a windfall after having snapped up shares at firesale prices in 2024 at the bankruptcy liquidation of collapsed crypto exchange FTX. Those include the quant giant Jane Street, which spent $1.34 billion to purchase Anthropic shares at the time—a stake that is likely to be worth over $35 billion after the IPO. And, in a twist of fate, Jane Street is the first employer of Sam Bankman-Fried, the disgraced founder of FTX, who is now serving a 25-year sentence for fraud in federal prison.

Bankman-Fried expressed frustration over the sale in a recent interview with The New York Times , criticizing the bankruptcy administrators who took control of FTX after its collapse. In addition to Jane Street, other buyers of FTX’s Anthropic shares are an investment vehicle linked to Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala and the Ford Foundation, both of which are also poised to share in the windfall.

Bankman-Fried became one of Anthropic’s earliest investors in late 2021, when he put $500 million into the little-known startup for a 13.5% stake that later shrank as the company raised more money, according to The New York Times .

Nearly five years later, Anthropic is just two days away from pricing what could be one of the largest initial public offerings in history, with trading on the Nasdaq expected to begin Thursday. Its proposed price range of $70 to $78 per share would value the company at up to roughly $1.4 trillion . The company behind the Claude chatbot generated $17 billion in revenue in the third quarter alone, up from $1.4…
